plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single three-dimensional drawing of a right circular cone, shaded in translucent teal with its apex at the top and an elliptical base at the bottom, cut by four dashed lines that each mark a different slicing plane. Near the apex a short, nearly horizontal dashed segment crossing a lightly shaded band is labeled 'Circle'. Below it a dashed line tilted modestly from horizontal passes through both sides of the cone and is labeled 'Ellipse'. A steeper dashed line runs from the upper left side of the cone down through the base and carries the label 'Parabola'. The fourth dashed line is nearly vertical, dropping through the right portion of the cone to the base, and is labeled 'Hyperbola'. Each cut has a correspondingly shaded region rendered inside the translucent solid, so the section surface itself is visible rather than just the cutting line, and all four labels are stacked along the right edge. Steepening the cut progressively from horizontal to vertical is the entire visual argument: one surface yields all four curves depending only on the inclination of the plane. The drawing collects the family of paths that an inverse-square force allows, the closed circle and ellipse alongside the open parabola and hyperbola.

elements: single upright right circular cone with apex at the top and circular base at the bottom
translucent teal conical side surface
translucent darker teal elliptical-looking base disk
central vertical cone axis, implicit but available for computing cuts
circle cutting plane near the apex, nearly horizontal, shown as a small lightly shaded planar slice
circle intersection curve on the cone, drawn as a short dashed dark oval/ellipse in screen view
label text 'Circle' to the upper right of the small horizontal cut
ellipse cutting plane below the circle, tilted moderately downward from left to right, shown as a translucent shaded slice through the cone
ellipse intersection curve on the cone, drawn as a larger dashed dark oval/ellipse in screen view
label text 'Ellipse' to the right of the tilted middle cut
parabola cutting plane, steeply inclined from upper right toward lower left so it is parallel to one side generator of the cone, shown as a tall translucent shaded slice running down to the base
parabola intersection curve, drawn as a dashed dark open curve/edge on the cone and visually represented in the source by a steep dashed line crossing the cone interior
label text 'Parabola' to the right of the steep central cut
hyperbola cutting plane, nearly vertical near the right side of the cone, shown as a narrow translucent shaded slice extending down through the base
hyperbola intersection curve/branch, drawn as a dashed dark open curve near the right flank of the cone
label text 'Hyperbola' to the right of the near-vertical cut
four stacked right-side labels aligned beside their corresponding cuts
dashed black styling for all intersection curves
soft internal teal-gray shaded regions showing each cutting plane inside the transparent cone

interactions.label: Cutting-plane angle
interactions.teaches: Changing only the inclination of one plane changes the cone section from a circle to an ellipse, then to the limiting parabolic case, and finally to an open hyperbolic branch

interactions.label: Named conic cut
interactions.teaches: Each orbit family corresponds to a specific relation between the cutting plane and the cone: closed cuts give circle or ellipse, while steeper cuts give the open parabola and hyperbola
Rotating the translucent cone makes clear that the dashed curves are true plane intersections on a three-dimensional cone, not separate two-dimensional curves drawn on the page

demo_steps.title: Circle: plane parallel to the base
demo_steps.narration: The slicing plane is horizontal, so every point on the intersection is the same distance from the cone axis. The section is a circle, seen in perspective as a small dashed oval near the apex.

demo_steps.title: Ellipse: tilted but still closed
demo_steps.narration: Tilting the plane produces a longer closed loop. Because the plane is not yet parallel to the cone side, it still cuts all the way around one nappe of the cone, forming an ellipse.

demo_steps.title: Parabola: limiting open cut
demo_steps.narration: At the critical angle the plane is parallel to a generator of the cone. The closed ellipse opens into the boundary case: a parabola.

demo_steps.title: Hyperbola: steeper than the cone side
demo_steps.narration: A still steeper plane cuts through the cone in an open branch. In the full double-cone construction the same plane would meet the opposite nappe to complete the hyperbola.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a single upright cone matching the source figure: apex at (0, 2.4, 0), base center at (0, -2.4, 0), height 4.8 units, base radius 1.65 units. +X is screen-right, +Y is screen-up, +Z is depth away from the viewer. Cone axis is vertical along Y. The source view is nearly front-on but slightly from above/right, so the circular base appears as a wide ellipse. Cone material: translucent teal/cyan, approximately #5fbfc0 at 0.38 opacity, with darker overlapping shaded facets #2f8f8f at 0.25-0.35 opacity. Base disk should be slightly darker teal #3ca5a5 at about 0.45 opacity. Intersections are black or very dark gray #111111 dashed curves, thin but visible. Labels are black, sans-serif, placed outside the cone on the right, stacked top to bottom: Circle near y≈1.85, Ellipse near y≈1.25, Parabola near y≈0.65, Hyperbola near y≈-0.65. Circle reference cut: plane angle 0° relative to the base/horizontal, positioned high near y≈1.72, small radius about 0.23-0.30 units. Ellipse reference cut: angle about 22° relative to the base, centered around y≈1.05, descending visually from left-high to right-low, intersection spanning roughly 1.0 unit across. Parabola reference cut: critical angle about 68° relative to the base/horizontal, visually a steep dashed trace running from upper central/right region down toward the lower left/base; this angle equals the side-generator angle because cone half-angle from vertical is atan(1.65/4.8)≈19°, so side angle from horizontal is about 71°; use 68-71° as the parabolic threshold for visual match. Hyperbola reference cut: angle about 82° relative to horizontal, nearly vertical, positioned on the right half of the cone, with dashed trace descending toward the base near x≈0.8. All cutting-plane patches should be clipped to the interior of the finite cone and rendered as translucent gray-teal slices, with the selected one brighter and the other three faded when the namedConicCut toggle is active.
interactionPlan.notes: Compute the active plane-cone intersection procedurally from the current cuttingPlaneAngle and clip to the finite cone height. Keep four faint reference cuts in the scene to preserve the textbook figure layout; when namedConicCut changes, emphasize the corresponding reference plane, curve, and label while fading the others. The slider should update the active highlighted plane continuously; crossing the circle/ellipse/parabola/hyperbola thresholds should update the visual classification label. Render dashed curves with THREE.LineDashedMaterial or segmented short line geometry on top of the transparent cone to avoid depth-fighting. Use polygon clipping or sampled implicit-curve points for plane patches; exact analytic conic perfection is less important than visibly preserving the circle-to-ellipse-to-parabola-to-hyperbola progression.

authoredContext:
One of the real triumphs of Newton’s law of universal gravitation, with the force proportional to the inverse of the distance squared, is that when it is combined with his second law, the solution for the path of any satellite is a conic section. Every path taken by m is one of the four conic sections: a circle or an ellipse for bound or closed orbits, or a parabola or hyperbola for unbounded or open orbits. These conic sections are shown in the figure.

All motion caused by an inverse square force is one of the four conic sections and is determined by the energy and direction of the moving body.

A cone and its conic sections is shown. At the top a horizontal cut is shaded and a dashed line shown across the shading. This section is labeled circle. Below this a diagonal cut and line are shown. The line and cut intersect the sides of the cone. This section is labeled ellipse. Next is a diagonal cut and line that intersect the sides and the bottom of the cone and are labeled parabola. The last section is a vertical line and shaded cut labeled hyperbola

If the total energy is negative, then 0≤e<1, and the equation represents a bound or closed orbit of either an ellipse or a circle, where e=0. [You can see from the equation that for e=0, r=α, and hence the radius is constant.] For ellipses, the eccentricity is related to how oblong the ellipse appears. A circle has zero eccentricity, whereas a very long, drawn-out ellipse has an eccentricity near one.

discrepancies: The parabola and hyperbola section curves are too faint and visually hard to distinguish compared with the clearly dashed black curves in the source.
The generated figure emphasizes one active section with a bright/solid-looking cut and bold label, whereas the source presents all four conic sections simultaneously with similar visual weight.
Labels are placed partly over the cone and faded for inactive sections; in the source the labels are clear black annotations to the right of the cone.
The cutting planes, especially for parabola and hyperbola, appear more like broad translucent patches with ambiguous boundaries rather than the distinct shaded planar slices shown in the source.
The cone is viewed more symmetrically/frontally than the source, reducing the strong textbook-style oblique perspective and making some internal section geometry harder to read.
evaluation.notes: The main cone, four conic-section cuts, colors, and labels are recognizable and the interactions are useful, but inactive curves and labels are too faint and the default emphasis differs from the source.
action_items: Make all four conic-section curves clearly visible with black dashed styling similar to the source, not heavily faded when inactive.
Move the labels farther to the right of the cone and keep them consistently dark and readable rather than fading inactive labels.
Adjust the default camera to better match the source's oblique textbook view, with the cone leaning visually left-to-right and the base ellipse more prominent.
Clarify the shaded cutting planes so each slice has a distinct boundary and resembles the planar cross-section panels in the source.
